name: Sliced Indexes (s_indexes)
baseline: Partitioned Elias-Fano (ds2i-style PEF); Roaring also compared
workload: Average microseconds per intersection of two compressed lists, 1,000 random pairs repeated 10 times, on the Census-Income, Census-1881, Weather and Wikileaks datasets shipped with CRoaring; bits per integer also reported.
claimed_speedup: Intersection time Slicing vs PEF (microseconds): Census-Income 11.56 vs 115.17, Census-1881 0.18 vs 0.92, Weather 25.70 vs 213.00, Wikileaks 0.47 vs 2.51; about 5x to 10x faster than PEF (derived from page data). Versus Roaring it is slower on 3 of 4 datasets (11.56 vs 4.68, 0.18 vs 0.15, 25.70 vs 13.37) and faster on Wikileaks (0.47 vs 0.86).
hardware: Intel i7-7700 @3.6 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Linux 4.4.0
tradeoffs: Uses more space than PEF on all four datasets (bits per integer 2.23 vs 2.03, 10.83 vs 7.28, 4.05 vs 3.13, 10.18 vs 8.87 for Slicing vs PEF) but is smaller than Roaring on all four. Targets bitmaps and inverted lists, not general rank/select. Needs AVX/SIMD-capable CPU for the fast paths (-march=native).
caveats: Baseline is PEF, which is an Elias-Fano structure, not SDSL or sux, so baseline_in_list is false. Slicing loses to Roaring on most of the README datasets, so the win is against the succinct (PEF) incumbent only. Two-list intersection only; the README table is the only evidence page opened. Author's own benchmark on old hardware and gcc 7.3.
found_via: GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/elias-fano?l=c%2B%2B led to jermp repos; opened README of jermp/s_indexes

name: rankselect (PTSelect, splatlab)
workload: Rank and select queries on uncompressed bit vectors, plus select on single 64-bit words using PDEP and TZCNT (PTSelect); the repo has bitmap_bench.cc and bitmap_bench_sdsl.cc that time the same queries on this code and on SDSL.
claimed_speedup: From the search-result snippet of the accompanying arXiv paper 1706.00990 (page not opened, snippet only): PTSelect about 4x faster than the previous select on machine words; select on bit vectors 2.2x to 6x faster than CS-Poppy and SDSL, and about 5x faster than CS-Poppy and 3x faster than SDSL for larger bit vectors.
tradeoffs: Select via PDEP needs a Haswell-or-later x86 CPU (BMI2). Rank/select over uncompressed bit sequences only. Bundles an old copy of SDSL headers for the comparison.
caveats: Speedup numbers come only from a search snippet of the paper (arXiv is blocked here), so they are not verified on an opened page. The README is one line with no numbers. CPU model is not stated in the files opened. Older SDSL version (2017). Newer work (pasta bit_vector, sux) is already catalogued and likely faster.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'A Fast x86 Implementation of Select PTSelect github' pointed to github.com/splatlab/rankselect; opened repo page, Makefile and bitmap_bench_sdsl.cc

name: mutable_rank_select
baseline: Fenwick-tree based rank/select over mutable bitmaps (Marchini and Vigna, now part of sux)
workload: rank, select, flip and access on a mutable bitmap, using a SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512) b-ary Segment-Tree index over 256- or 512-bit blocks.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the Information Systems 2021 paper (page not opened, snippet only): the Segment-Tree is consistently faster than solutions based on the Fenwick tree. No ratio recorded.
compiler_and_flags: Tested with gcc 7.4 and 9.2.1 and clang 10/11; README recommends cmake Release with -DDISABLE_AVX=Off -DAVX512=On (exact flags in CMakeLists.txt, not opened)
tradeoffs: Supports updates (flip), unlike static SDSL/pasta structures. Needs AVX2 or AVX-512 for best speed. Space is higher than a static rank/select directory.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (tier B), but the speedup is qualitative and comes from a snippet; the README itself has no numbers and the paper hosts (ScienceDirect, arXiv) are blocked. Baseline is the Fenwick tree design now inside the already-catalogued vigna/sux, so this may count as evidence about sux rather than a new baseline.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/rank-select?l=c%2B%2B; WebSearch 'Rank/Select Queries over Mutable Bitmaps' for the paper claim

name: pwm (parallel wavelet tree and matrix construction)
baseline: Shun's wavelet tree construction (DCC 2015) and Labeit et al.; SDSL-based competitors can be built with PWM_BUILD_SDSL_WT
workload: Construction of wavelet trees and wavelet matrices from text, sequential and parallel (up to 32 cores); also an external-memory variant.
claimed_speedup: Search-result snippet of the ALENEX 2018 abstract (page not opened, snippet only): sequential algorithm up to twice as fast as the currently fastest sequential construction (Shun, DCC 2015) while saving a factor 2 in space; parallel algorithm scales to 32 cores with performance comparable to Labeit et al. using about 75% of the space.
tradeoffs: Construction only: it builds the tree faster and in less space, it does not change query speed. Output format differs from sdsl wt classes.
caveats: The repo README has no numbers and names no SDSL speedup; SDSL is only an optional competitor build. The claim is against other construction algorithms, not against SDSL's constructor, so it is weak for the SDSL baseline. Numbers are from a snippet. Compiler, flags and CPU not seen.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ wavelet matrix wavelet tree library faster than sdsl-lite'; github.com/topics/wavelet-tree?l=c%2B%2B

name: wavelet_forest
baseline: SDSL Huffman-shaped wavelet tree (sdsl-lite), uncompressed bitvectors
workload: access queries (10,000 random positions) on synthetic multi-GB texts over bit, base-4, octal, hex and ASCII alphabets; wavelet forest built with fixed block sizes from 50 KB to 10 MB versus one global wavelet tree.
claimed_speedup: README, no numbers: wavelet forest 'often outperforms' the wavelet tree on larger alphabets (ASCII); faster for hex across a broad range of block sizes; blocks of about 0.5 MB frequently best; speedups are not monotonic in block size.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from cache locality of per-block trees; the README tests uncompressed bitvectors only, so space behavior with compressed bitvectors is not shown. Per-block alphabets and metadata add overhead. Targets access, with rank 'often'.
caveats: Tier B rests on the peer-reviewed SPIRE 2024 paper 'Another Virtue of Wavelet Forests' (Springer page not opened); the README has no numeric results or hardware, so the size of the win is unverified. Research-grade code; GPL-3.0.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github C++ wavelet matrix wavelet tree library faster than sdsl-lite' returned the repo; opened the README
